newsitem.title: INDIA: India's PM, chief justice debate role of judges.
newsitem.headline: India's PM, chief justice debate role of judges.

text.p: India's prime minister and top judge traded polite barbs on Friday in a public debate over the role of activist judges who are viewed with apprehension by the country's politicians.

At stake in the debate between Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Chief Justice J.S. Verma was public interest litigation (PIL), a decade-old legal weapon that has helped judges probe political corruption and attack administrative red tape.
Gujral said he wondered if India's judges were going too far in pushing politicians to act, and Verma retorted it was perhaps because people thought politicians were not going far enough.

"Is it (PIL) distorted? Is it not? Is it something moving in the right direction?," Gujral said while inaugurating a national convention of lawyers to mark 50 years of India's independence from British colonial rule.
Leading politicians have been entangled in a web of corruption trials and federal investigators have been goaded to act faster by PIL cases, often filed by opposition groups or independent activists.

An Indian judge can even treat a postcard as a formal petition or voluntarily take note of a problem if he believes administrators, investigators and politicians are not acting in the public interest.
Verma, who heads India's Supreme Court, has himself entertained PIL petitions. He said judges may have been forced by public pressure to consider PILs.
"The primary purpose of a PIL is to make every authority do what they are needed for, and do it themselves," he said. "We don't want to enter a sphere where we are not needed."
"Everyone seems to be running to the courts for every problem which cannot be solved elsewhere," Verma said.
Gujral, calling upon lawyers to examine the role of the judiciary, chose his words carefully.
"I am very much afraid of what they call contempt of court," he said.
"We feel the relationship between the legislature and the judiciary is such that it is sometimes comfortable, sometimes not so comfortable," Gujral said earlier in his speech.
The prime minister emphasised justice for the poor. "We...feel concerned about equity," he said, seeking speedier disposal of court cases.
India's judiciary had a backlog of more than 25 million cases, Law Minister Ramakant Khalap told the same conference.

"We have a mesh of law, and a cobweb of procedures and the common man feels like an insect caught in the cobweb," Khalap said, adding that judges often blamed politicians and bureaucrats for social problems.
"The judiciary, from the high pulpits, holds these organs of the democracy responsible for every malaise the country suffers from," Khalap said.
Justice Verma said both judges and administrators should do their jobs with concern for their duties.
"Only if you think of it as a power, it becomes a problem," he said. "What he (Gujral) meant to say was that there must be a spirit of accommodation," he added.
